fetched_contents.text: Short- and long-term cardiovascular outcomes in insulin-treated versus non-insulin-treated diabetes mellitus patients after percutaneous coronary intervention: A systematic review and meta-analysis Abstract Aims This study aims to assess differences in severity of short-term (<1 year) and long-term (≥1 year) adverse CV outcomes after PCI in insulin-treated vs. non-insulin-treated diabetes mellitus (DM) patients. Methods A systematic search on Pubmed and Embase led to the incorporation of 29 studies that compared post-percutaneous coronary interventional outcomes in insulin-treated and non-insulin-treated diabetes mellitus. Diabetes mellitus (type 2) was defined as fasting blood glucose (FBG) level of >7.0 mmol/L or with an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) level of >11.1 mmol/L at least on two separate occasions. Adverse CV outcomes were assessed in insulin-treated and non-insulin-treated DM after the PCI procedure considered for the analyses were mortality, MACE, TLR, TVR, MI, stent thrombosis, target lesion failure (TLF), and need for-post PCI CABG. Data were pooled and analyzed using Review Manager 5.3, and risk ratios (RR) with respective 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated.The statistical analyses were carried out by Review Manager v.5.3, and the data were pooled using a random-effects model. Risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were reported along with forest plots. The chi-square test was performed to assess for differences between the subgroups. Heterogeneity across studies was evaluated using Higgins I2 statistics. Visual inspection of the funnel plot and Begg's regression test were used to assess publication bias. Results A total of 40,527 patients (11742 in the Insulin-treated diabetes mellitus group and 28785 in the non-insulin-treated DM group) who underwent PCI were included. The pooled analysis of short-term follow up outcomes preceding PCI demonstrated a significantly higher risk of mortality (RR = 1.75 [1.24,2.47]; p = 0.002), MI (RR = 1.81[1.14,2.87]; p = 0.01], stent thrombosis (RR = 1.63[1.13, 2.35]; p = 0.009) and target lesion revascularization (TLR) (RR = 1.29[1.02,1.63]; p = 0.03) in insulin-treated DM patients. Similarly, analysis of long-term follow-up studies depicted a significantly higher risk mortality (RR = 1.55 [1.22, 1.97]; p = 0.0003), MI (RR = 1.63 [1.35, 1.97]; p=<0.00001), MACE (R = 1.47 [1.31, 1.65]; p=<0.00001), stent thrombosis (RR = 1.54 [1.19,1.99]; p = 0.001), TLR (RR = 1.40 [1.18, 1.66]; p = 0.0001), target vessel revascularization (TVR) (RR = 1.35 [1.11, 1.64]; p = 0.003) in insulin-treated DM group after PCI versus non-insulin-treated DM patients. Conclusion Despite a tremendous technical success rate of multi-vessel stenting, people living with diabetes who were being treated with insulin had higher long-term, and short-term mortality rates, MI, TLR, TVR, and stroke compared to people living with diabetes who were being treated with means other than insulin and are more prone to detrimental cardiovascular outcomes. Introduction As the current consumer lifestyle is becoming increasingly sedentary, the world faces an epidemic of ‘diabetes mellitus (DM)’ with more than 171 million people affected worldwide.1 It is one of the most common chronic medical conditions known for its progressive nature; DM poses a severe public health challenge in the twenty-first century. Initially, DM is managed through dietary modification and oral hypoglycemic drugs; an intensification of therapy is generally required as the disease progresses over the years rendering insulin addition to the regimen a necessity.2 It is well-established that cardiovascular (CV) complications are the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in people living with diabetes; hence standard practice involves aggressive risk factor control, yet approximately 20–30% of patients require percutaneous coronary interventions (PCI) at some point during the disease.3 There is currently conflicting evidence about the severity of adverse CV outcomes following PCI in diabetic populations treated with insulin compared to those with diabetes who have not received insulin therapy.4, 5, 6 Several studies have shown that the risk of adverse outcomes like target lesion failure (TLF) and target lesion revascularization (TLR) after PCI is higher in insulin-treated people living with diabetes than in non-insulin-treated people living with diabetes.3,6 However, other studies have concluded that the increased risk of adverse cardiovascular (CV) outcomes is only present until propensity score has been adjusted. Moreover, the frequency of stent thrombosis and mortality rates after stent placement were also found to be comparable in both groups i.e. insulin-treated patients living with diabetes and non-insulin-treated patients living with diabetes.7,8 Therefore, with the aim to standardize the issue, conclude the current debate and, further evaluate the risk of wide range of CV events in insulin-treated versus non-insulin-treated patients living with diabetes, we assessed short-term (<1 year) and long-term (≥1 year) adverse CV outcomes after PCI in both the aforementioned groups. Authors Affiliations * 1 Institute of Cardiovascular Diseases, The First Affiliated Hospital of Guangxi Medical University, Nanning, Guangxi, 530027, People's Republic of China. pravesh021@gmail.com. * 2 Institute of Cardiovascular Diseases, The First Affiliated Hospital of Guangxi Medical University, Nanning, Guangxi, 530027, People's Republic of China. 120159659@qq.com. * 3 Institute of Cardiovascular Diseases, The First Affiliated Hospital of Guangxi Medical University, Nanning, Guangxi, 530027, People's Republic of China. xyicucmh@sina.com. * PMID: 26446829 * PMCID: PMC4597459 * DOI: 10.1186/s12933-015-0300-6 Abstract Background: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (DM) patients have worse adverse cardiovascular outcomes after Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI). However, the adverse cardiovascular outcomes between insulin-treated and non-insulin treated DM patients have been a subject of debate. We sought to compare the short-term (<1 year) and long-term (≥1 year) cardiovascular outcomes between insulin-treated and non-insulin treated DM patients after PCI. Methods: Medline and Embase databases were searched for studies by typing 'diabetes and percutaneous coronary intervention/PCI' or 'insulin-treated and non-insulin treated diabetes mellitus and PCI'. Endpoints included adverse cardiovascular outcomes reported in these DM patients during the corresponding follow-up periods. Odd Ratio (OR) with 95% confidence interval (CI) was used to express the pooled effect on discontinuous variables and the pooled analyses were performed with RevMan 5.3. Results: 21 studies have been included in this meta-analysis consisting of a total of 21,759 diabetic patients (6250 insulin-treated and 15,509 non-insulin treated DM patients). Short term mortality, myocardial infarction, target lesion revascularization, major adverse cardiac effects and, stent thrombosis were significantly higher in insulin-treated diabetic patients (OR 1.69, 95% CI 1.40-2.04, p < 0.00001), (OR 1.40, 95% CI 1.16-1.70, p = 0.0005), (OR 1.37, 95% CI 1.06-1.76, p = 0.02), (OR 1.46, 95% CI 1.22-1.76, p < 0.0001) and (OR 1.66, 95% CI 1.16-2.38, p = 0.005) respectively. Long-term cardiovascular outcomes were also significantly higher in insulin-treated DM patients. Conclusion: Insulin treatment in these DM patients was associated with a significantly higher short and long-term adverse cardiovascular outcomes after PCI compared to those DM patients not treated by insulin therapy. fetched_contents.text: Short-Term Versus Long-Term Adverse Cardiovascular Outcomes Post Percutaneous Coronary Intervention in Patients with Insulin-Treated Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus: A Simple Meta-Analysis Abstract Introduction Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a major health issue, especially in patients with coexisting coronary artery disease (CAD). Patients with insulin-treated T2DM (ITDM) have worse outcomes than those with non-insulin-treated T2DM. Very few studies have compared short-term to long-term adverse cardiovascular outcomes following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) in patients on insulin therapy. Therefore, in this meta-analysis, we systematically compared short-term to long-term adverse cardiovascular outcomes in a population of patients with ITDM following PCI. Methods We searched for English-language publications focusing on PCI in patients with ITDM using specific search terms/phrases. All the participants accepted for inclusion in this meta-analysis were treated with a drug-eluting stent. Post-intervention adverse cardiovascular outcomes observed during short-term and long-term follow-up periods were assessed and compared. Statistical analysis was carried out using the popular RevMan 5.3 software. Odd ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. Results Six studies comprising 1568 participants with ITDM in total were included in this simple meta-analysis. Patient enrollment periods varied but enrollment occurred during the years 1993–2012. When a fixed-effects statistical model was used, post-PCI adverse cardiovascular outcomes—such as major adverse cardiac events (MACEs) (OR 3.33, 95% CI 2.64–4.21; P = 0.00001), all-cause mortality (OR 5.73, 95% CI 3.37–9.73; P = 0.00001), myocardial infarction (MI) (OR 1.47, 95% CI 1.05–2.07; P = 0.02), and repeated revascularization (OR 4.78, 95% CI 3.29–6.94; P = 0.00001)—were found to be significantly more likely during the long-term follow-up period. A similar result was observed with a random-effects statistical model. Conclusion Adverse cardiovascular outcomes post PCI were significantly more likely during the long-term follow-up period than during the short-term follow-up period in these patients with T2DM on insulin therapy. This hypothesis requires confirmation via new comparative trials that consider short-term and long-term follow-up periods. Complicated T2DM can lead to sudden cardiac death, silent myocardial infarction, and stroke [2, 3]. Patients with insulin-treated T2DM (ITDM) have worse outcomes than those without insulin therapy following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) [4]. fetched_contents.title: Comparing the adverse clinical outcomes in patients with non-insulin treated type 2 diabetes mellitus and patients without type 2 diabetes mellitus following percutaneous coronary intervention: a systematic review and meta-analysis - PMC
fetched_contents.text: Comparing the adverse clinical outcomes in patients with non-insulin treated type 2 diabetes mellitus and patients without type 2 diabetes mellitus following percutaneous coronary intervention: a systematic review and meta-analysis Abstract Background Several studies showed Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) to be associated with worse adverse clinical outcomes compared to non-T2DM (NDM) following Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI). In addition, patients with insulin-treated T2DM (ITDM) showed worse clinical outcomes compared to patients with non-insulin treated T2DM (NITDM). Since NITDM and NDM have seldom been systematically analyzed, this study aimed to compare the short and long term adverse clinical outcomes observed in patients with NITDM and patients without T2DM following PCI. Methods Medline/PubMed, EMBASE and the Cochrane library were searched for Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) and observational studies comparing patients with (including ITDM and NITDM) and without T2DM following PCI. Endpoints included adverse clinical outcomes reported during a short and a long term follow up period. Odd Ratios (OR) and 95% Confidence Intervals (CI) in accordance with either a fixed or a random effects model appropriately, were calculated and the pooled analyses were performed with RevMan 5.3. Results Twelve studies consisting of a total number of 52,451 patients (14,863 NITDM and 37,588 NDM) were included. Patients with NITDM were found to have significantly higher short-term Major Adverse Cardiac Events (MACEs) and mortality with OR: 1.63, 95% CI (1.17, 2.27); P = 0.004 and OR: 1.71, 95% CI (1.40, 2.10), P < 0.00001 respectively and higher long-term MACEs and mortality with OR: 1.25, 95% CI (1.12, 1.40), P = 0.0001 and OR: 1.32, 95% CI (1.19, 1.47), P < 0.00001 respectively compared to NDM following PCI. In addition, compared to NDM, long-term Target Vessel Revascularization (TVR) and Target Lesion Revascularization (TLR) were significantly higher in the NITDM group with OR: 1.36, 95% CI (1.18, 1.56), P < 0.0001 and OR: 1.32, 95% CI (1.10, 1.59), P = 0.003 respectively. However, even if an increased long-term stent thrombosis was observed in the NITDM group with OR: 1.13; 95% CI (0.91, 1.40), P = 0.28, the result was insignificant. Conclusion Short and long term MACEs and mortality were significantly higher in patients with NITDM compared to patients without diabetes following PCI. Revascularization also significantly favored patients without T2DM. However, stent thrombosis was not significantly different. Keywords: Non-insulin treated diabetes mellitus, Percutaneous coronary intervention, Major adverse cardiac events, Stent thrombosis, Clinical outcomes Background Patients with Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) have worse clinical outcomes compared to patients without T2DM (NDM) following Percutaneous Coronary Intervention (PCI). For example, the PRESTO trial showed that despite advances in interventional techniques, diabetes mellitus remained a significant predictor of adverse clinical events after PCI [1, 2]. Later on, it was shown that patients with insulin-treated T2DM (ITDM) had even worse adverse outcomes compared to patients with non-insulin treated T2DM (NITDM). To further illustrate this point, the FREEDOM trial showed a significantly higher rate of Major Adverse Cardiac Effects (MACEs) in those diabetic patients who were on insulin therapy following PCI compared to those patients without insulin therapy [2]. It is clear that patients without T2DM when compared to patients with T2DM and patients with NITDM compared to ITDM have lower adverse clinical events following PCI. Since NITDM and NDM have seldom been systematically analyzed, this study aimed to compare the short and long term adverse clinical outcomes observed in patients with NITDM and patients without T2DM following PCI. Methods Data sources and search strategy Studies including Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs) and observational studies were searched from Medline/PubMed, EMBASE and the Cochrane databases using the words ‘diabetes mellitus and percutaneous coronary intervention/PCI’ or ‘insulin-treated and non-insulin treated diabetes mellitus and PCI’. The term ‘angioplasty’ and the abbreviations ‘T2DM and DM’ were also used. Reference lists of relevant publications obtained were also checked for suitable articles. Our search began on 2nd May 2015 and ended on 30th September 2015. This search was restricted only to articles which were published in English language. Inclusion and exclusion criteria Studies were included if: 1. They were randomized trials and observational studies comparing the adverse outcomes between T2DM (including ITDM and NITDM) and NDM following PCI. 2. They were published during or after the year 2006 (from the year 2006 to 2015). Studies were excluded if: 1. Data concerning patients with NITDM could not be retrieved from these diabetic patients. 2. Patients without T2DM were not included as the control. 3. Adverse clinical outcomes were not reported among their endpoints. 4. They were meta-analyses, case studies or letter to editors. 5. They were published before the year 2006. 6. They were duplicates. Definitions, outcomes and follow up periods NITDM were defined as patients who were at an earlier stage of T2DM, or did not have any diabetic complications or patients with a good control of their blood glucose levels, therefore not requiring insulin therapy as treatment. These patients were either on a diet control or on oral hypoglycemic agents. The adverse clinical outcomes were: 1. Mortality: defined as all-cause mortality including cardiac and non-cardiac deaths. 2. MACEs: were defined as death of cardiac or procedure-related origin, myocardial infarction, and/or, revascularization following coronary stents implantation. Overall comparative risk of adverse cardiovascular outcomes after PCI in insulin-treated vs non-insulin-treated T2DM patients

The evidence consistently suggests that, across the included studies, insulin-treated T2DM patients generally have higher short-term and long-term adverse cardiovascular outcomes after PCI compared with non-insulin-treated T2DM patients. The most direct evidence comes from a meta-analysis of 29 studies involving 40,527 patients, which reported significantly higher short-term mortality, MI, stent thrombosis, and TLR in insulin-treated DM patients [N1-F1]. A second meta-analysis of 21 studies involving 21,759 diabetic patients similarly found higher short-term mortality, MI, TLR, MACE, and stent thrombosis in insulin-treated diabetic patients [N2-F2]. Another meta-analysis of six studies involving 1,568 ITDM patients found long-term adverse cardiovascular outcomes—including MACE, all-cause mortality, MI, and repeated revascularization—to be significantly more likely in insulin-treated patients [N3-F3].

For specific outcomes, the evidence points to a pattern of elevated risk across the main adverse events typically assessed in PCI trials:
- **Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE)**: consistently higher in insulin-treated patients [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3]
- **Myocardial infarction (MI)**: consistently higher in insulin-treated patients [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3]
- **Stroke**: the meta-analysis explicitly cites stroke as a secondary outcome and the broader comparison statement notes higher stroke in insulin-treated patients [N1-F1]
- **Death**: both short-term and long-term mortality were significantly higher in insulin-treated patients [N1-F1][N2-F2]
- **Stent thrombosis**: significantly higher in insulin-treated patients in the first meta-analysis, while the second meta-analysis found only long-term stent thrombosis was higher in insulin-treated diabetic patients [N1-F1][N2-F2]
- **Revascularization outcomes**: TLR and TVR were significantly higher in insulin-treated patients in both meta-analyses [N1-F1][N2-F2]

The direction of the association is not uniform across all designs and populations. The evidence indicates that some studies show higher risk in insulin-treated patients, while other studies or subgroup analyses suggest that this difference may be attenuated or even disappear after adjustment for confounding factors [N1-F1][N4-F4]. In particular, the meta-analysis notes that some studies showed higher risk only after propensity score adjustment, and that stent thrombosis and mortality rates were comparable in some comparisons [N1-F1]. The non-insulin-treated T2DM vs non-diabetic comparison meta-analysis also found that NITDM patients had higher short-term and long-term MACE and mortality compared to non-diabetic patients [N4-F4], but this is a separate comparison that still implies that insulin-treated patients may face worse outcomes than non-insulin-treated patients within T2DM.

Study-level heterogeneity is clearly present. The first meta-analysis pooled 29 studies and used a random-effects model, with I2 statistics indicating heterogeneity, and it reported differences in the subgroups of short-term versus long-term outcomes [N1-F1]. The second meta-analysis also pooled 21 studies, with a random-effects model and comparable risk ratios [N2-F2]. The third meta-analysis, which focused specifically on insulin-treated T2DM patients, pooled only six studies and found significant associations with a fixed-effects model, but the report itself notes that this finding requires confirmation in new trials [N3-F3]. Taken together, the results are not entirely consistent across cohorts, but they broadly converge on a higher risk in insulin-treated T2DM patients for most adverse cardiovascular outcomes after PCI, especially when the comparison is against non-insulin-treated T2DM patients [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F4].

In summary, the evidence supports the conclusion that insulin-treated T2DM patients generally have higher adverse cardiovascular outcomes after PCI than non-insulin-treated T2DM patients, but the strength and consistency of the association vary by study design and population, and some subgroup analyses or adjusted comparisons show less clear separation [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F4].

Outcome definitions, adverse events, and how outcomes are measured

Across the evidence provided, adverse cardiovascular outcomes after PCI are defined and measured in a somewhat standardized but not fully uniform way across studies. The main adverse events captured in the studies are **myocardial infarction (MI)**, **stroke**, **death**, **stent thrombosis**, and **revascularization outcomes** such as **target lesion revascularization (TLR)**, **target vessel revascularization (TVR)**, and **target lesion failure (TLF)**. In the first meta-analysis, the primary adverse CV outcomes were death, MACE, TLR, TVR, MI, and stent thrombosis, while stroke was a secondary outcome [N1-F1]. In the second meta-analysis, the endpoints included short-term mortality, MI, TLR, MACE, and stent thrombosis [N2-F2]. The non-insulin-treated T2DM vs non-diabetic comparison also notes that outcomes may be influenced by confounding because the pooled analysis used observational studies and appropriate fixed or random effects models [N4-F4]. Second, **selection bias and heterogeneous patient selection** are important. The non-insulin-treated T2DM vs non-diabetic comparison defines NITDM as patients with earlier-stage T2DM, no diabetic complications, and good glucose control not requiring insulin [N4-F4]. This shows that diabetes classification is not purely based on diagnosis but also on treatment and disease stage, which can introduce selection bias. The broader evidence also suggests that PCI indication and case selection differ, and that diabetes status affects PCI outcomes [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4]. Because the evidence comes from heterogeneous studies, including registry-based analyses and observational designs, the comparison is likely to be affected by differences in patient selection rather than a single uniform effect [N1-F1][N4-F4].

Third, **heterogeneous outcome definitions** are a significant limitation. The studies capture a common core of adverse events—myocardial infarction, stroke, death, stent thrombosis, and revascularization outcomes—but they do not all use identical definitions or adjudication criteria. The non-insulin-treated T2DM vs non-diabetic comparison explicitly defines mortality and MACE, and notes that MACCEs were analyzed in the same category as MACEs when outcomes were limited [N4-F4]. The broader meta-analysis evidence also shows that outcomes are often reported as risk ratios or odds ratios with confidence intervals, using software such as RevMan [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3]. This heterogeneity makes direct comparison across studies difficult and limits the ability to draw a single robust conclusion.

Fourth, **study-level inconsistency** is evident. The evidence shows that some studies report higher risk in insulin-treated patients, while other studies or subgroup analyses suggest that the difference may be attenuated or disappear after adjustment [N1-F1][N4-F4]. The first meta-analysis pooled 29 studies and used a random-effects model, with I2 statistics indicating heterogeneity [N1-F1]. The second meta-analysis pooled 21 studies with a random-effects model [N2-F2]. Taken together, the results are not entirely consistent across cohorts, and the direction of the association may depend on study design, population, and adjustment method [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F4].

Fifth, **subgroup findings are inconsistent and context-dependent**. However, the provided evidence does not provide precise subgroup risk ratios for all modifiers, and some findings are indirect or based on comparisons with non-diabetic controls rather than head-to-head insulin-treated vs non-insulin-treated comparisons [N11]. This means the results are context-dependent rather than universally generalizable.

### 6) Clinical implications for PCI decision-making and diabetes management

The clinical implications are important and practical. First, the evidence suggests that **insulin-treated T2DM patients may face higher adverse cardiovascular risk after PCI compared with non-insulin-treated T2DM patients**, but this is not uniform across all studies and populations [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F4]. This means that PCI decision-making should not assume a single, uniform risk profile for all T2DM patients and should account for insulin status.

Second, **glycemic control and diabetes management** are relevant confounders. Better glycemic control after PCI may improve long-term outcomes in diabetic patients [N4-R5]. Therefore, diabetes management should be optimized before and after PCI, especially in insulin-treated patients who may have more complex metabolic profiles.

Third, **propensity adjustment and observational methods** are important to account for confounding, especially when comparing insulin-treated and non-insulin-treated patients [N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R3]. This suggests that crude comparisons may not be sufficient for clinical inference, and that adjusted analyses are often needed to reduce bias.

This means that clinical interpretation should be cautious in patients with renal impairment or heavy comorbidity, as these factors may alter the observed insulin-treated vs non-insulin-treated difference [N11].

Fifth, **duration of diabetes and time since diagnosis** may affect outcomes, but the evidence provided does not establish precise insulin-treated vs non-insulin-treated risk estimates by these factors [N6-R1][N6-R2]. Therefore, clinicians should be aware that longer diabetes duration may increase risk, but this should not be interpreted as a universal rule without further direct comparison.

### 7) Bottom line

In conclusion, the evidence across systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and observational studies generally supports the conclusion that **insulin-treated patients with T2DM have higher adverse cardiovascular outcomes after PCI than non-insulin-treated T2DM patients**, especially for MI, mortality, stent thrombosis, and revascularization [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-F4]. However, the evidence is not definitive and is affected by confounding, heterogeneous outcome definitions, study-level heterogeneity, and context-dependent subgroup differences [N1-F1][N4-F4][N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R3][N11]. Clinically, the implications are that PCI decision-making and diabetes management should be informed by insulin status, glycemic control, comorbidity, renal function, and the need for propensity adjustment [N1-F1][N4-F4][N4-R5][N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R3]. The direction of the association is not uniform across all designs and populations. ## Integrated synthesis: How adverse cardiovascular outcomes after PCI compare between insulin-treated and non-insulin-treated T2DM patients across studies

The overall evidence across systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and observational studies suggests that **insulin-treated patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) generally have higher adverse cardiovascular outcomes after percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)** than non-insulin-treated T2DM patients, but the strength and consistency of this association vary by study design, population, and adjustment method [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3][N4-F4].

### 1) Overall comparative risk: insulin-treated vs non-insulin-treated T2DM

The most direct evidence comes from three meta-analyses that consistently point in the same general direction. One meta-analysis of 29 studies involving 40,527 patients reported significantly higher short-term mortality, MI, stent thrombosis, and TLR in insulin-treated DM patients [N1-F1]. A second meta-analysis of 21 studies involving 21,759 diabetic patients also found higher short-term mortality, MI, TLR, MACE, and stent thrombosis in insulin-treated diabetic patients [N2-F2]. A third meta-analysis of six studies involving 1,568 insulin-treated T2DM patients found significantly higher long-term MACE, all-cause mortality, MI, and repeated revascularization [N3-F3]. In addition, a separate comparison of non-insulin-treated T2DM (NITDM) vs non-diabetic patients found that NITDM patients had higher short-term and long-term MACEs and mortality than non-diabetic patients [N4-F4].

For the main adverse events, the evidence consistently supports elevated risk in insulin-treated patients:
- **Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE)**: higher in insulin-treated patients [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3]
- **Myocardial infarction (MI)**: higher in insulin-treated patients [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-F3]
- **Stroke**: the broader evidence indicates higher stroke in insulin-treated patients, and stroke is explicitly noted as a secondary outcome in the first meta-analysis [N1-F1]
- **Death**: both short-term and long-term mortality were significantly higher in insulin-treated patients [N1-F1][N2-F2]
- **Stent thrombosis**: higher in insulin-treated patients in some studies, though not always statistically significant across all analyses [N1-F1][N2-F2]
- **Revascularization outcomes**: TLR and TVR were significantly higher in insulin-treated patients in the meta-analyses [N1-F1][N2-F2]

However, the direction of the association is not uniform across all designs and populations. The evidence indicates that some studies show higher risk in insulin-treated patients, while other studies or subgroup analyses suggest that this difference may be attenuated or disappear after adjustment for confounding factors [N1-F1][N4-F4]. In particular, the first meta-analysis notes that some studies showed higher risk only after propensity score adjustment, and that stent thrombosis and mortality rates were comparable in some comparisons [N1-F1]. The non-insulin-treated T2DM vs non-diabetic comparison also found that NITDM patients had higher short-term and long-term MACEs and mortality compared to non-diabetic patients [N4-F4]. Taken together, the evidence supports a general pattern of higher adverse outcomes in insulin-treated T2DM patients, but the association is not universally consistent across cohorts [N1-F1][N2-F2][N4-F4].

### 2) Outcome definitions, adverse events, and how outcomes are measured

Across the evidence, adverse cardiovascular outcomes after PCI are defined and measured in a somewhat standardized but not fully uniform way. The main adverse events captured in the studies are **myocardial infarction (MI)**, **stroke**, **death**, **stent thrombosis**, and **revascularization outcomes** such as **target lesion revascularization (TLR)**, **target vessel revascularization (TVR)**, and **target lesion failure (TLF)**. In the first meta-analysis, the primary adverse CV outcomes were death, MACE, TLR, TVR, MI, and stent thrombosis, while stroke was a secondary outcome [N1-F1]. In the second meta-analysis, the endpoints included short-term mortality, MI, TLR, MACE, and stent thrombosis [N2-F2]. In the third meta-analysis, the main outcomes were MACE, all-cause mortality, MI, and repeated revascularization, with stroke mentioned as a secondary outcome [N3-F3]. In the non-insulin-treated T2DM vs non-diabetic comparison, the adverse clinical outcomes were defined as mortality and MACE, with MACE defined as death of cardiac or procedure-related origin, MI, and/or revascularization following coronary stents implantation [N4-F4].

The temporal framing of outcomes varies by study. The first meta-analysis distinguishes **short-term (<1 year)** and **long-term (≥1 year)** adverse outcomes [N1-F1]. The second meta-analysis also distinguishes short-term and long-term cardiovascular outcomes [N2-F2]. The third meta-analysis compares **short-term** to **long-term** adverse cardiovascular outcomes in insulin-treated T2DM patients [N3-F3]. The non-insulin-treated T2DM vs non-diabetic comparison also reports **short-term** and **long-term** adverse outcomes [N4-F4].
